## 3-Letter Jotto: Let's Play {.activity .smaller}

**The setup:**

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="15%"}
```
DEW  FOX  GEL  INK
JOG  MOB  NAP  NIP
NOR  NUT  OAT  OIL
PUG  SOY  WOO  YAK
```
:::
:::

- There are 16 possible secret words -- you choose one.
- I guess a word; You respond with the count of letters in common (0, 1, or 2). If I get 3, the game is over!
- I will continue to guess until I guess your word.

**The Play:** Turn and face the back of the room.

## What Strategy Did You Discover?

Discussion questions:

- What makes a "good" first guess?
- What happens if you guess NAP, then NIP, then NUT?
- Can you **always** win in 2 guesses? Why or why not?

::: notes
Lead into: the strategy IS a tree! Each guess partitions the remaining words by their Jotto score. Good guesses split evenly. Bad guesses leave big partitions.

Lower bound discussion: Each guess has 3 branching outcomes (0, 1, or 2 matches). Getting 3 matches means you guessed correctly—game over, no more branches needed! So with 3 outcomes per guess and 16 words, theoretically log₃(16) ≈ 2.5 guesses should suffice. Since we can't make half a guess, the lower bound is 3 guesses. But even that's hard to achieve in practice!
:::

## Why Trees?

Trees appear everywhere in computer science:

| Domain | Tree Structure |
|--------|---------------|
| File systems | Directories contain subdirectories |
| HTML/DOM | Elements contain child elements |
| Decision making | Each choice leads to sub-choices |
| Classification | "Is it X? If yes, go left..." |
| Game AI | Possible moves branch into more moves |

## Trees: The Most Important Nonlinear Structure {.smaller}

> "Trees are the most important nonlinear structure in computer science."
>
> — Donald Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*

:::
::: {.column width="65%"}
- One of the vertices is called the [root]{.red} of the tree. Guess which one it is.
- Make an English word containing the names of the vertices that have a [parent]{.red} but no [sibling]{.red}.
- How many [parents]{.red} does each vertex have?
- Which vertex has the fewest [children]{.red}?
- Which vertex has the most [ancestors]{.red}? [descendants]{.red}?
- What is d's [depth]{.red}? What is d's [height]{.red}?
- List all the vertices in b's left [subtree]{.red}.
- List all the [leaves]{.red} in the tree.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="65%"}
- [root]{.red}: the single node with no parent
- [leaf]{.red}: a node with no children
- [child]{.red}: a node pointed to by me
- [parent]{.red}: the node that points to me
- [sibling]{.red}: another child of my parent
- [ancestor]{.red}: my parent or my parent's ancestor
- [descendant]{.red}: my child or my child's descendant
- [subtree]{.red}: a node and its descendants
- [depth]{.red} of node x: number of edges on path from root to x
- [height]{.red} of node x: number of edges on longest path from x to a leaf
:::
:::

## *d-ary* Tree Definition

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
A **d-ary tree** T is either:

- \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

OR

- \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 260 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width: 240px;">
  <!-- A 3-ary tree with ~10 nodes, each subtree of root a different color -->

  <!-- Middle subtree (green) -->
  <!-- Right subtree (blue) -->

  <line x1="130" y1="25" x2="210" y2="75" stroke="#0077b6" stroke-width="2"/>

  <!-- Left subtree edges (red) -->
  <line x1="50" y1="95" x2="25" y2="145" stroke="#d62828" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="50" y1="95" x2="75" y2="145" stroke="#d62828" stroke-width="2"/>

  <!-- Middle subtree edges (green) -->
```

:::

::: notes
Fill in via annotation:
- Empty (no nodes)
- A root node with up to d subtrees (each a d-ary tree)

Binary tree = d-ary tree with d=2

The tree shown has d=3 (ternary). Each subtree of the root is colored differently to emphasize the recursive structure.
:::

:::

::: notes
This is a matching activity. Students should draw lines connecting:
- Perfect Tree: All levels completely filled (coral tree, top) - this is both full AND complete
- Complete Tree: All levels filled except possibly the last, which is filled left-to-right (teal tree, middle)
- Full Tree: Every node has 0 or 2 children (yellow tree, bottom) - note it can be unbalanced!

Key insight: Perfect ⊂ Complete, and Perfect ⊂ Full, but Complete and Full are independent properties.
:::

## Week 8 Summary

- Trees are **hierarchical** structures with a root, children, and leaves
- **Binary trees** have at most 2 children per node
- Trees are **recursively defined**: a tree is empty OR a root with subtrees
- Tree **terminology**: root, leaf, parent, child, sibling, ancestor, descendant, depth, height
- **Decision trees** model sequences of choices
